opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core question is basically a race between two forces. On one side, once you've fully automated AI research, you get a big increase in the effective labor going into improving AI: you can run huge numbers of copies, they work fast, they don't sleep. And those AIs are themselves improving the algorithms that make the next generation of AIs better. That's a feedback loop. On the other side, ideas get harder to find. Each additional improvement in, say, algorithmic efficiency tends to require more research effort than the last one. So the question is whether the returns to research effort are good enough that the feedback loop outpaces that diminishing returns.

The way I'd approach this empirically is to look at historical data on algorithmic progress. You ask: over some period, how much did the effective research input grow, in terms of researcher headcount and compute for experiments, and how much did the efficiency of training or inference improve? From that you can back out a rough estimate of the returns to research. If, roughly speaking, doubling cumulative research input gets you more than a doubling in the effective capability of your AI workforce, then progress will tend to accelerate after full automation, at least until you hit some other limit. If it gets you less than a doubling, the loop fizzles out and you get a burst followed by a slowdown.

My read of the evidence, which is pretty uncertain, is that the returns look like they're plausibly above that threshold, maybe somewhat above it. That suggests you'd get a period of accelerating progress, potentially quite fast, rather than a smooth continuation of current trends. But there are big caveats.

One is compute. Right now a lot of AI progress is bottlenecked on running experiments, not just on having smart researchers think. If compute is roughly fixed in the short run, then even with tons of automated researchers, you might be bottlenecked on experiments. How much smarter and more numerous researchers can substitute for compute is a really key parameter, and we don't have great data on it. I think there's a decent amount of substitutability: better researchers can run smaller, more informative experiments, pick better ideas, waste less compute on bugs. But it's not unlimited.

Another is that the historical estimates come from a regime with human researchers, and it's not obvious they extrapolate cleanly. There might be low-hanging fruit that AIs can grab that humans couldn't, which would push toward faster progress. Or we might be approaching some limits on how efficient algorithms can get, which would slow things down eventually.

And then there's just the question of how far you are from those limits. Even if the feedback loop eventually slows, if there's a lot of room to go, you could still get an enormous amount of progress in a short period, potentially years' worth or more of what would otherwise be a decade's progress.

So putting it together: I think it's more likely than not that progress speeds up meaningfully after full automation, and there's a substantial chance it's very rapid. But I'd put real weight on scenarios where compute bottlenecks or diminishing returns make it a more modest acceleration. And I think that uncertainty matters a lot for planning, because the fast scenarios are the ones where we have the least time to notice problems and respond.

r001.rationale: It describes AI researchers improving the algorithms that make later AIs better, creating a feedback loop that can speed progress.

r002.rationale: It identifies ideas becoming harder to find and each additional improvement requiring more research effort as a counterforce.

r003.rationale: It proposes comparing historical researcher headcount and experimental compute with gains in training or inference efficiency to estimate research returns.

r004.rationale: It tentatively judges that progress is more likely than not to accelerate meaningfully after full automation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to look at is the dynamics of the research process once you've got AI systems that can do everything a human researcher could do. And the way I'd frame it is: there's basically a race between two forces. On one side, you've got AI systems making progress on AI research, which produces more capable systems, which then do research faster, and so on. That's the feedback loop that would get you acceleration. On the other side, you've got the problem getting harder over time — each successive improvement is harder to find than the last one, diminishing returns in the research itself.

So the question is really: as you double the effective amount of research effort, how much does that improve the system? And then, how much harder does the next doubling get? If each doubling of cumulative research effort gets you more than enough improvement to speed up the next doubling by a corresponding amount, you get acceleration — potentially pretty explosive acceleration. If it's less than that, things slow down and eventually plateau, at least until you add more compute or something.

The empirical way I'd try to get at this is to look at the historical relationship between inputs and outputs in AI research. Like, how much have we needed to grow the number of researchers, and the amount of compute, to sustain the rate of algorithmic progress we've seen? There's work from Epoch and others trying to estimate algorithmic efficiency gains over time, and you can compare that against how fast the labour force and compute budgets have grown. My read of the evidence is that it's somewhat ambiguous, but it leans toward the view that returns to research effort are high enough that you'd get at least a substantial speedup initially — maybe a lot more than that.

I want to flag a few caveats though. One is that compute is a real bottleneck. Even if you have vastly more AI researchers, if they're all competing for the same experiments on the same GPUs, that constrains things a lot. So a big part of my assessment hinges on how much you can substitute labour for compute — can really smart researchers get the same information from much smaller experiments? I think the answer is somewhat yes, but it's not unlimited.

The second caveat is that "full automation" is doing a lot of work in that question. In practice I expect we'll go through a period where AI is automating a bunch of tasks but not all of them, and the remaining human-bottlenecked parts limit the overall speedup. By the time you're actually at full automation, the systems are probably already substantially superhuman at a lot of things, and the dynamics could already be quite fast.

And the third thing is that I think you should just have really wide uncertainty here. Like, I'd put real probability on things going relatively quickly — a year or so of really rapid progress getting you to systems that are wildly beyond human level — and also real probability on it being much slower and more bottlenecked than that. If I had to give a central guess, I'd say a speedup that's more than a few times and plausibly much more, with the tail risk on the fast side being the thing I think people should take most seriously from a safety perspective.

r001.rationale: It describes AI systems improving AI research, producing more capable systems that then research faster—a reinforcing feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It identifies the research problem getting harder over time and diminishing returns as a force countering acceleration.

r003.rationale: It proposes comparing historical researcher and compute growth with algorithmic progress to assess how much research effort produces progress.

r004.rationale: It tentatively expects at least a substantial initial speedup, while acknowledging uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how the returns to doing more research compare with the difficulty of making further progress. Full automation could let you put vastly more effective effort into AI research, but that doesn’t by itself tell you whether you get a sustained acceleration.

There are two effects pulling in opposite directions. Better AI systems can do research more efficiently, which helps you build still better systems. But the improvements you’re looking for might get harder to find as you pick the low-hanging fruit. And some research requires experiments that take substantial compute or elapsed time, so having more researchers doesn’t necessarily make everything proportionally faster.

I’d want to distinguish a big initial speedup from what happens after that. You could automate research, get a burst of progress by scaling up the amount of work, and then settle into a slower trajectory because experiments become the bottleneck. Or the improvements could make both the researchers and their experiments sufficiently more efficient that the feedback loop keeps strengthening.

So I’d look at how much progress you get from additional research effort, how quickly that return declines, and how much each improvement increases your capacity to do further research. I think substantial acceleration is quite plausible, but full automation alone doesn’t establish that progress will keep accelerating.

r001.rationale: It says better AI systems can do research more efficiently, helping build still better systems, and describes this as a potentially strengthening feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It identifies low-hanging fruit being picked and returns to additional research effort declining as forces that could slow acceleration.

r003.rationale: It does not propose using the historical relationship between human research labour and effective compute progress to estimate AI research returns.

r004.rationale: It presents an initial burst of progress as one possible scenario and says substantial acceleration is plausible, but does not affirmatively judge that progress will initially accelerate after full automation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions. One is: how much faster can you do research if you automate the work people are currently doing? And the other is: how quickly does that faster research produce systems that are even better at doing research?

For the first question, you could get a substantial speedup just from having many copies working in parallel, running continuously, and potentially thinking faster than humans. But you shouldn’t assume that a thousand times as much research labour gives you a thousand times as much progress. Experiments take time, compute is scarce, and some research depends on sequential steps where you need one result before you can figure out what to do next.

For the second question, the key issue is the returns to improving the researcher. If each improvement lets you find the next improvement substantially faster, you can get a very rapid feedback loop. If improvements get harder to find, or mostly require larger training runs, then that loop could be much weaker.

So I’d look at how much progress comes from ideas versus additional compute, how well research parallelises, and how long the experiments take. Full automation seems like a strong reason to expect acceleration, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether that means a large one-off increase in the rate of progress or an increasingly rapid intelligence explosion.

r001.rationale: It describes a feedback loop where improvements to AI researchers can help them find the next improvement faster.

r002.rationale: It says improvements may get harder to find, weakening the acceleration loop.

r003.rationale: It discusses ideas versus compute, but does not propose using historical links between human research labour and effective compute progress to estimate AI research labour returns.

r004.rationale: It says full automation is a strong reason to expect research acceleration, while noting the acceleration could be a one-off increase or an increasingly rapid loop.
